Liquid ammonia presents advantages as an energy carrier, particularly considering its mass density, volumetric energy density, volumetric hydrogen content, and storage pressure. Liquid ammonia is unfavorable in terms of gravimetric energy density, gravimetric hydrogen content, and energy required to extract H . 2 Ammonia has also been considered as a H carrier for fuel cells. Ammonia can be thermally 2 decomposed or catalytically cracked to form H , which can be used in a fuel cell. Other research 2 is looking at the direct use of ammonia in various types of fuel cells. Proton exchange membrane fuel cells are not a good candidate for a direct ammonia system as they require 12 COMPARISON OF COMMERCIAL, STATE-OF-THE-ART, FOSSIL-BASED AMMONIA PRODUCTION ammonia-free H and ammonia content exceeding 0.1 ppm can poison the cell membrane and 2 catalyst (U.S. DOE, 2006). Solid oxide fuel cells can decompose ammonia without poisoning their ceramic electrolytes due to their high operating temperatures (Cheddie, 2012). At temperatures greater than 700 °C, the performance of ammonia-fed solid oxide fuel cells may approach that of hydrogen-fed solid oxide fuel cells (Cheddie, 2012). Finally, alkaline fuel cells are tolerant to ammonia; however, due to low operating temperatures, pre-processing is required to generate H first (Cheddie, 2012). 2 Ammonia’s low flammability, high NOx emissions, and low radiation intensity present some challenges for utilizing ammonia for combustion; however, this is still an active area of research and development. The Department of Energy/Fossil Energy has funded programs that are conducting research on H /NH combustion fundamentals for gas turbines. For combustion 2 3 turbines, Japan’s Fukushima Renewable Energy Institute and the Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology are looking at a 50-kWe gas turbine fueled with pure ammonia that successfully generated 41.8 kWe of power (Kobayashi, et al., 2018). Japan’s Central Research Institute of Electric Power Industry is studying the co-firing of pulverized coal and ammonia using a horizontal test furnace (Kobayashi, et al., 2018). Their RD&D determined that ammonia may act as both a selective non-catalytic reduction additive and as a fuel for heat release, depending on the ratio of ammonia to coal and the location of injection (Kobayashi, et al., 2018).
